statements: The chief complaint is a two-week history of unilateral left lower extremity swelling and pain.
The patient’s immediate concern is likely a vascular cause such as deep venous thrombosis.
The case data quickly redirect away from primary venous thrombosis and toward a pelvic obstructive process.
Salient positive findings include unilateral left leg pitting edema and pain.
Salient positive findings include slight improvement with elevation and NSAIDs.
Salient positive findings include a Doppler ultrasound negative for DVT.
Salient positive findings include CTA showing a large heterogeneous left pelvic retroperitoneal mass centered at the left iliac chain measuring 8.7 × 6.9 × 8.5 cm.
Salient positive findings include probable compression or occlusion of the adjacent iliac vein.
She has elevated inflammatory markers.
Her ESR is 35 mm/hr.
Her CRP is 30.1 mg/L.
Her age is 65 years.
Her age raises concern for malignancy.
She is immunomodulated with methotrexate and adalimumab for inflammatory polyarthritis.
This immunomodulatory therapy broadens concern for lymphoproliferative disease.
The diagnosis must rest on the presented findings.
Strong peripheral pulses argue against arterial insufficiency as the cause of leg symptoms.
The abdomen being soft and nondistended does not exclude a retroperitoneal pelvic mass.
There is no shortness of breath.
There is no chest pain.
The absence of shortness of breath and chest pain makes pulmonary embolism less likely as the explanation for symptoms.
There is no recent trauma.
The absence of recent trauma argues against hematoma from injury.
There is no fever.
The absence of fever makes abscess or infectious adenitis less likely.
There is no unexplained weight loss.
The absence of unexplained weight loss does not exclude malignancy.
She is on therapeutic warfarin.
Therapeutic warfarin with a negative Doppler makes standard lower-extremity DVT less likely as the primary diagnosis.
The smoking history is minimal and remote.
The smoking history does not strongly point toward a smoking-related metastatic malignancy.
The first differential is deep venous thrombosis.
Deep venous thrombosis fits unilateral leg swelling and pain.
Deep venous thrombosis is undermined by a negative Doppler ultrasound.
Deep venous thrombosis is undermined by the discovery of a large pelvic mass directly compressing or occluding the iliac vein.
Deep venous thrombosis could still coexist proximally.
The imaging provides a more direct explanation than deep venous thrombosis.
The next differential is lymphoma.
Lymphoma is plausible because the mass is centered at the left iliac chain, where bulky nodal disease can occur.
Lymphoma is plausible because inflammatory markers are elevated.
Immunosuppressive therapy makes lymphoproliferative disease a reasonable consideration.
The imaging description emphasizes a large heterogeneous retroperitoneal pelvic mass rather than clearly nodal conglomerates.
There are no B symptoms reported.
Retroperitoneal sarcoma is another strong candidate.
Retroperitoneal sarcoma fits an older adult with a large heterogeneous retroperitoneal mass causing mass effect on the iliac vein and resulting unilateral leg edema.
Sarcomas commonly present as large masses due to the expansile capacity of the retroperitoneum.
Sarcomas may lack systemic symptoms early.
Ovarian neoplasm is also considered.
A pelvic mass in a woman can arise from adnexal structures and cause venous compression.
The lesion is described as retroperitoneal and centered at the left iliac chain rather than clearly adnexal.
There are no gynecologic or abdominal symptoms provided.
Germ cell tumor is much less likely in a 65-year-old woman.
Germ cell tumor was included in the imaging differential.
The age and location make germ cell tumor less favored.
The patient’s leg swelling is best explained by iliac vein compression from a pelvic retroperitoneal mass.

Among the candidate etiologies listed, the imaging description of a large heterogeneous retroperitoneal mass in an older adult most strongly favors retroperitoneal sarcoma over lymphoma or ovarian neoplasm.
The most likely diagnosis is retroperitoneal sarcoma presenting with left iliac vein compression and unilateral leg edema.
The differential diagnosis includes retroperitoneal sarcoma with high likelihood.
Retroperitoneal sarcoma is supported by a large heterogeneous left pelvic retroperitoneal mass measuring 8.7 × 6.9 × 8.5 cm in a 65-year-old.
Retroperitoneal sarcoma is supported by probable iliac vein compression or occlusion and unilateral leg edema.
Retroperitoneal sarcomas often present as bulky masses with mass effect.
The differential diagnosis includes lymphoma with medium likelihood.
Lymphoma is supported by a mass centered at the left iliac chain.
Lymphoma is supported by elevated ESR and CRP.
Immunomodulatory therapy may increase concern for lymphoproliferative disease.
No B symptoms are reported.
The differential diagnosis includes ovarian neoplasm with low likelihood.
A pelvic mass in an older woman could be adnexal and cause venous compression.
The imaging describes a retroperitoneal mass centered at the iliac chain rather than a clearly ovarian lesion.
The differential diagnosis includes deep venous thrombosis with low likelihood.
Unilateral painful pitting edema suggests DVT.
Doppler ultrasound was negative.
CTA identified a pelvic mass with probable iliac vein compression as a more direct cause.
The final diagnosis is retroperitoneal sarcoma.
